text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London stayed lower by the close in a sluggish session with the market seen heading for a bout of range trading, dealers said. Benchmark May closed $5 down at $1,570 a tonne after trading between $1,567 and $1,581.
Traders said the market's upside potential is now limited with volume and volatility fast dwindling. The May/July spread narrowed to $6 by the close from $10 on Monday.

Arabica futures in New York finished mainly weaker in thin, directionless dealings, pressured by light speculative selling, traders said. A lack of fresh fundamental news contributed to the sluggish tone, with the local activity on both sides of the market confining prices to a narrow range.

May closed down 0.65 cents/lb, at 178.75 cents/lb, after trading from 180.80 to 176.00. Second month July settled 0.55 cents/lb weaker, at 164.50 cents/lb, while the back months finished 1.90 lower to 3.50 firmer. The closely watched May/July switch, which widened to around 15.00 cents during the session, ended at 14.25 cents, down slightly from 14.35 cents at the close the previous day.
Technically, traders pegged May support at 175.00 cents, then 172.00-171.00 cents. Resistance was seen at 183.00-183.50, followed by 185.00.
After the close the CSCE reported certified coffee stocks were off 500 60-kg bags, to 81,828 bags as of April 7. There were no bags pending grading, the exchange said.

GUATEMALA - Guatemala exported 577,000 60-kg bags of coffee in March, the Guatemalan Coffee Association (Anacafe) announced. The exports are slightly up on the same month last year, when the country exported 547,000 bags. In total, Guatemala has now exported 2.736 mn bags of coffee in the current 1996/97 campaign (October/September), up 32 per cent from the tonnage shipped the previous year. Anacafe officials said earlier that the country exported most of its coffee at the start of the harvest, when prices were high. Now there is little coffee left to ship, officials added.

TANZANIA - Tanzania's northern arabica coffee production could fall to as low as 167,000 60-kg bags for the 1997/98 season because of a severe drought which hit much of East Africa, government and industry officials said. Northern arabica production in the 1996 season totalled about 267,000 bags, according to official statistics. Jeremy Lefroy, the secretary of the Tanzania Coffee Association (TCA) told Reuters that the only glimmer of hope lay in a good coffee harvest forecast for the country's southern arabica region which could help offset the expected production deficit in the north. Total arabica production in 1996/97 (July/June) is estimated at around 505,000 bags, down from 689,000 bags in 1995/96.

UNITED STATES - Coffee imports in January 1997 amounted to 1.720 mn bags, down from the 1.941 mn bags imported in January 1996. Total imports in 1996 reached 19.434 mn bags, up from 17.105 mn bags in 1995. Major suppliers of green coffee in January 1997 were Mexico (425,400 vs 556,300 bags), Guatemala (198,800 vs 195,800 bags), Colombia (192,600 vs 281,200 bags) and Brazil (190,200 vs 63,100 bags). Coffee exports in January 1997 reached 184,831 bags, up from 114,765 bags in January 1996. Total exports in 1996 amounted to 2.047 mn bags compared to 1.841 mn bags in 1995. US exports of coffee are mainly in the form of solubles with Hong Kong (13,600 vs nil bags) and South Korea (13,400 vs 5,600 bags) featuring as the main markets in January 1997.
